questions.question_text: A hospital records the waiting time of every one of the $3140$ patients it saw in March and finds the mean waiting time is $27$ minutes. Which statement is correct?

options.text: $27$ minutes is a parameter, because it describes every member of the population.
$27$ minutes is a statistic, because it was worked out from collected data.
options.why: Treats every calculated number as a statistic; a parameter is calculated too, just from the whole population.

options.text: $27$ minutes is a statistic, because $3140$ patients is far too many to be a population.
options.why: Uses the size of the group to decide, but a population may contain millions of members.

options.text: $27$ minutes is a parameter, because $3140$ patients is large enough to count as a population.
options.why: Uses the size of the group to decide; whether a value is a parameter depends on whether it describes the whole population, not on how large the group is.

questions.solution_text:
The population is all $3140$ patients seen in March.
Every one of them was included.
A number describing the whole population is a **parameter**.

questions.question_text: A researcher measures the fuel use of all $46$ buses in a depot and finds the standard deviation is $2.3$ L/100 km. Which is the correct notation?

options.text: $\sigma=2.3$

options.why: Uses the sample standard deviation symbol although every bus in the population was measured.
Uses the population mean symbol for a standard deviation.
Uses the sample mean symbol, wrong on both counts: it is a standard deviation and it describes the population.

questions.solution_text:
All $46$ buses is the whole population, so a population symbol is needed.
The number is a standard deviation.
$\sigma=2.3$

questions.question_text: A council tests $25$ of the $900$ streetlights in a suburb to estimate how many of the suburb's streetlights need replacing. What is the population?

options.text: All $900$ streetlights in the suburb.
The $25$ streetlights that were tested.
options.why: Names the sample rather than the population.

options.text: The streetlights in the suburb that need replacing.
options.why: Names the characteristic being counted rather than the group being investigated.

options.text: All streetlights in the state.
options.why: Widens the population beyond the group the council is investigating.

questions.solution_text:
The council wants to know about the streetlights in the suburb.
That group is every individual being studied.
Population: all $900$ streetlights in the suburb.

questions.question_text: A random sample of $60$ eggs has standard deviation $s=3.1$ g. Which quantity is $s$ an estimate of?

options.text: $\sigma$, the standard deviation of all the eggs in the population.
$\mu$, the mean mass of all the eggs in the population.
options.why: Matches the sample standard deviation to the population mean instead of the population standard deviation.

options.text: $\bar{x}$, the mean mass of the $60$ eggs sampled.
options.why: Names another sample statistic; a statistic estimates a population value, not a second statistic.

options.text: $n$, the number of eggs in the sample.
options.why: Names the sample size, which is known exactly and needs no estimating.

questions.solution_text:
$s$ is the standard deviation of a sample.
Each sample statistic estimates the matching population parameter.
$s$ estimates $\sigma$.

questions.question_text: Three separate random samples of $200$ households each give mean weekly water use of $412$ L, $427$ L and $405$ L. Which statement best explains the three different values?

options.text: A sample mean changes from sample to sample, while the population mean is a single fixed number.
The population mean changed between the three surveys.
options.why: Treats the parameter as varying; it is fixed, and only the statistic changes.

options.text: At least two of the three samples must have been collected incorrectly.
options.why: Treats natural sample-to-sample variation as an error in the data collection.

options.text: The largest value, $427$ L, must be the population mean.
options.why: Assumes one sample gives the parameter exactly, and picks it by size rather than by any reasoning.

questions.solution_text:
The population mean is a parameter, so it is one fixed number.
Each sample mean is a statistic, worked out from whichever $200$ households were chosen.
Different households give different sample means.

questions.question_text: Every student who sat an exam had a mean mark of $74$ with standard deviation $11$. A random sample of $30$ of those students had a mean mark of $76$ with standard deviation $9$. Which line correctly records the **sample** values?

options.why: Uses the sample symbols but attaches the population's numbers to them.
Records the sample's numbers with the population symbols.
Correct notation, but for the population rather than the sample the question asks about.

questions.solution_text:
The sample of $30$ students had mean $76$ and standard deviation $9$.
Sample values use $\bar{x}$ and $s$.
$\bar{x}=76$, $s=9$

questions.question_text: A rope maker tests $12$ ropes to destruction, chosen at random from a batch of $4000$, in order to estimate the mean breaking strain of the batch. Which quantity is the parameter of interest?

options.text: The mean breaking strain of all $4000$ ropes in the batch.
The mean breaking strain of the $12$ ropes tested.
options.why: This is the statistic that was measured, not the population value it estimates.

options.text: The number of ropes tested, $12$.
options.why: Names the sample size rather than the quantity being estimated.

options.text: The mean breaking strain of every rope the maker has ever produced.
options.why: Uses a population wider than the batch the investigation is about.

questions.solution_text:
The investigation is about the batch of $4000$ ropes.
The quantity wanted for that whole group is its mean breaking strain.
That population value is the parameter.

questions.question_text: A national sports body wants the mean training time of all registered junior swimmers. It obtains the training time of every one of the $84$ swimmers at one club (mean $9.4$ hours per week) and of $650$ registered swimmers chosen at random nationally (mean $8.7$ hours per week). Which statement is correct for the sports body's investigation?

options.text: Both $9.4$ and $8.7$ are statistics, because each describes only part of the registered junior swimmers.
$9.4$ is a parameter and $8.7$ is a statistic, because every swimmer at the club was included.
options.why: Treats a census of the club as a census of the population; the club is only part of the body's population.

options.text: Both $9.4$ and $8.7$ are parameters, because both were worked out from data that was actually collected.
options.why: Treats any number obtained from real data as a parameter, ignoring which group it describes.

options.text: $8.7$ is a parameter and $9.4$ is a statistic, because $650$ is the larger group.
options.why: Uses the size of the group to decide; size never makes a sample into a population.

questions.solution_text:
The population is all registered junior swimmers in the country.
The $84$ club swimmers are every member of the club, but only part of that population.
The $650$ swimmers surveyed are also only part of it.
A number describing part of the population is a statistic, so both values are **statistics**.
